hypotheses.text: Recessive biallelic RNU2-2 variants exhibit a significantly earlier median age of seizure onset (infancy, median 10.5 to 18 months) and higher rates of epileptic spasms / tonic seizures compared to dominant de novo RNU2-2 variants.
hypotheses.rationale: Greene et al. (2025) originally noted dominant de novo RNU2-2 cases presented with complex epilepsy, while emerging cohorts of biallelic RNU2-2 cases (Henry et al. 2026; Leitão et al. 2026) report median seizure onsets around 10.5 to 18 months with high frequencies of infantile spasms and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome-like phenotypes. Jackson et al. further assert that the recessive condition is clinically distinct from the dominant form.

evidence.text: In biallelic RNU2-2 individuals, onset of seizures showed an earlier median seizure-onset age of 10.5 months, with infantile spasms and tonic seizures being predominant seizure types and frequent progression to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome.

hypotheses.text: Epilepsy penetrance in dominant de novo RNU2-2 cases is virtually complete (>95%) while in biallelic recessive cases penetrance is incomplete (~80-85%), leaving a subset of recessive patients who present with intellectual disability without clinical seizures.
hypotheses.rationale: Greene et al. (2025) reported that all 25 dominant cases presented with a severe seizure phenotype (100% penetrance), whereas Leitão et al. (2026) documented that only 82% (72 of 88) of individuals with biallelic RNU2-2 variants developed seizures, demonstrating incomplete penetrance in the recessive cohort.

evidence.text: All 25 identified dominant de novo RNU2-2 individuals displayed a severe and complex seizure phenotype.

source.title: Mutations in the small nuclear RNA gene RNU2-2 cause a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent epilepsy
source.quote: All cases display a severe and complex seizure phenotype.

evidence.text: In individuals with biallelic RNU2-2 variants, 72 of 88 (82%) exhibited seizures, leaving 16 of 88 (18%) free of seizures at the time of evaluation.

source.title: Systematic analysis of snRNA genes reveals frequent RNU2-2 variants in dominant and recessive developmental and epileptic encephalopathies

hypotheses.text: The divergent epilepsy penetrance and severity between dominant and recessive RNU2-2 disorders are driven by distinct molecular mechanisms: dominant mutations act via a dominant-negative, toxic spliceosomal disruption, whereas recessive mutations cause quantitative loss of U2-2 snRNA transcript abundance.
hypotheses.rationale: Greene et al. (2025) observed mutant U2-2 expression without missplicing in blood for dominant cases, whereas Jackson et al. (2026) and Greene et al. (2026) demonstrated that biallelic variants cause transcript instability with >90% reduction in U2-2 abundance and altered U2-2/U2-1 ratios.

evidence.text: Biallelic variants correlate with reduced U2-2 abundance and compromised transcript stability, altering the ratio of U2-2 to U2-1, establishing a mechanism distinct from dominant RNU2-2 disorder.

source.title: Biallelic variants in RNU2-2 cause a remarkably frequent developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
source.quote: We find that candidate biallelic variants are significantly correlated with reduced U2-2 abundance, implicating compromised transcript stability as a probable pathomechanism. We identify a decreased ratio of U2-2 to its paralog U2-1 as a potential diagnostic biomarker for this condition. We show that the recessive RNU2-2 syndrome is genetically, clinically and mechanistically distinct from the dominant RNU2-2 disorder.

evidence.text: Whole-blood RNA sequencing in biallelic cases showed >90% reduction in expression of pathogenic U2-2 alleles, pointing to a loss-of-expression mechanism.

source.title: Biallelic variants in RNU2-2 cause the most prevalent known recessive neurodevelopmental disorder
source.quote: Whole-blood RNA sequencing data showed a >90% reduction in the expression of pathogenic U2-2 alleles in biallelic cases and monoallelic carriers, albeit with wild-type compensation in carriers, pointing to a loss-of-expression mechanism.

new_directions.question_text: Does the specific combination of compound heterozygous variants (e.g., promoter/loss-of-expression allele in trans with 5' core coding variant) modulate seizure onset and refractoriness in recessive RNU2-2 syndrome?
new_directions.rationale: Leitão et al. and Greene et al. found that recessive cases frequently harbor de novo mutations in trans with inherited alleles across varying domains of RNU2-2. Dissecting allelic series will test whether residual U2-2 expression correlates with the presence or absence of epilepsy.

new_directions.question_text: What is the detailed comparative seizure semiology and drug responsiveness between dominant de novo and biallelic RNU2-2 cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Henry et al. observed high rates of infantile spasms, tonic seizures, and Lennox-Gastaut patterns in biallelic patients. Evaluating whether dominant cases share these specific semiologies or respond differently to anti-seizure medications will clarify whether DEE119 clinical classification requires inheritance-stratified sub-phenotyping.
